newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasury's Summers slams estate tax opponents.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury's Summers slams estate tax opponents.

text.p: Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers slammed opponents of the U.S. tax system Monday, accusing them of "selfishness" and charging they want to "whip Americans into a frenzy."
Summers said most tax cuts should benefit middle income Americans instead of the very wealthy and singled out opponents of the inheritance tax for special criticism.

"I actually think in terms of substantive arguments this estate tax argument is about as bad as it gets," he told a group of reporters at a luncheon, noting the estates of only one percent of Americans are taxed.
"In the case of the estate tax, I think there is no case other selfishness," he said, contrasting it to the capital gains tax, where there was room for disagreement.
The administration is negotiating a tax and spending package with the Republican-led Congress. Summers said any final package must benefit middle income earners.
"I think the overall tax package has to have as its thrust helping middle class America," Summers said.
He strongly criticized those who have attacked the Internal Revenue Service, saying they unjustly sought to build opposition to the U.S. tax system.

"I think there has been a fairly active effort to whip them into a frenzy over (tax) issues with the agenda of delegitimizing government in general and delegitimizing progressive taxation in particular," he said.
Summers mentioned no names, but House Ways and Means Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, has said repeatedly he wants to pull up the IRS by the roots and abolish it.
And House Majority Leader Richard Armey, of Texas, is a strong advocate of abolishing the graduated income tax in favor of a flat tax.

Summers said there is room for improvement at the IRS, noting that one of its large shortcomings is poor telephone service to taxpayers, compared with the kind of service customers get from airlines or other large businesses.
But Summers said the U.S. tax system is more economical and effective than those of other large industrialized nations.
"The IRS has one of the lowest ratios of collection to cost" among industrialized nations, spending only 0.4 percent of each dollar it collects in administration costs, he said.
"There's a very important balance between seeing the need for change and at the same time recognizing that not everything's wrong," he said.
